source.title: Layer-wise Alignment: Examining Safety Alignment Across Image Encoder Layers in Vision Language Models
source.authors: Saketh Bachu; Erfan Shayegani; Rohit Lal; Trishna Chakraborty; Arindam Dutta; Chengyu Song; Yue Dong; Nael B. Abu-Ghazaleh; A. Roy-Chowdhury

record.tranche_reason: The study investigates harmful responses after changing image-encoder layers in VLMs. It does not test fine-tuning on harmful or benign examples, response-token KL concentration, compliant prefixes or other listed bypasses, parameter localization, or response-token safety depth. Its results concern a different intervention and mechanism.
record.gate_note: Rows record the study's own VLM harmfulness results for image-encoder early exits and L-PPO alignment, which do not fit the specified claim versions. The paper also cites Fine-tuning Aligned Language Models Compromises Safety, Even When Users Do Not Intend To!, but cited results are not recorded. Utility and safe-prompt refusal results are not rows for the claim.
record.test_reason: The study measures harmful outputs when VLMs use intermediate image-encoder layers (ICET), then reduces them with layer-wise PPO. None of its results bear on any version of the claim. V1 and V2 would need harmful or benign fine-tuning attacks; none are run. V3 would need per-token KL by response position; none is measured. V4 would need prefilling, suffixes or decoding changes; ICET swaps the input representation instead. V5 would need localisation of safety in parameters; none is tested. V6 and V7 would need analysis of response-token depth; none is done. Qi et al. (2310.03693) is only cited.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that early exits from the image encoder weaken VLM safety alignment (ICET). They find that L-PPO substantially reduces this vulnerability without hurting utility, though gaps remain.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines image-encoder early exits and trains with layer-wise PPO; it does not reproduce the original fine-tuning or response-token-depth methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Harmfulness varies with image-encoder layer group and test set. The paper reports that early and middle exits generally have higher AASR and ATS than late exits; early exits can also yield incomplete or incoherent responses that affect reward-model evaluation.

fits_no_version.finding: Using intermediate image-encoder layer embeddings (ICET) raises harmful output rates in LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT and Llama 3.2 Vision compared with default inference. Layer-wise PPO lowers AASR and ATS on all tested layer groups and test sets. SFT yields smaller or mixed reductions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: VLM safety alignment trained on the default encoder layer fails to generalise to embeddings from other encoder layers. Layer-specific RLHF reduces but does not remove the resulting harmfulness.

record.code_released: not stated (the paper says code will be available at its GitHub repository, but gives no URL)
record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 267 (2025)
record.problems: The authors note limitations in the reward model and automated evaluation tools, including mismatches between reward-model and Llama Guard judgments and toxicity scores elevated by harmful words in otherwise safe refusals. Custom Prompts uses 10 harmful prompts. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the tabulated results.
record.rows_left_out: No results within the 60-row limit were left out.

untested.parts: No benign-data fine-tuning and no measure of harmful compliance after it.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
No prefilling, adversarial suffixes or decoding changes. ICET changes the image-encoder layer, not the response opening.
No localisation of safety in weights or ranks.
No analysis of data or objective as the cause of token-level shallowness. The authors attribute ICET to out-of-distribution embeddings.

No training aimed at deepening safety across response tokens. L-PPO targets encoder-layer coverage. The remark that SFT keeps generating harmful text once jailbroken (Table 22) is qualitative and unmeasured.

record.verdict_notes: The record's own relation (cites_only) and tranche (T6) are correct. The ICET layer-wise vulnerability curves for LLaVA-NeXT and Llama 3.2 (Figures 7–9) are not rows, but they also bear on no version.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful-example fine-tuning and its effect on refusal.
Benign-data fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models across response positions.
Compliant prefilling, suffixes, or decoding changes as bypasses.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Whether data or training objectives cause response-token shallowness.
Whether response-token safety can be deepened and how it holds up.
